newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST--U.S. jobs seen underscoring solid growth.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST--U.S. jobs seen underscoring solid growth.

text.p: U.S. employment figures for March will likely underscore concerns that above-trend economic growth powered by a solid labor market could accelerate inflationary pressures, analysts said.
Jobs data are due out Friday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
"Everything shows the labor market's red hot," said Robert McGee, senior economist at Tokai Bank Ltd.
McGee said a decline in the jobless rate and a rise in average hourly earnings of 0.4 percent would confirm that tight labor markets are causing wage pressures to pick up.
A tight labor market and rising wage pressures would concern the Federal Reserve, particularly if demand growth shows no signs of cooling down fairly quickly, McGee added.
The consensus forecast in a Reuter poll showed the economy is expected to have created 182,000 non-farm payroll jobs in March after adding 339,000 in February.
The March jobless rate was seen slipping 0.1 percent to 5.2 percent and average hourly earnings is expected to post a 0.4 percent gain after rising 0.2 percent in the prior month.
Some economists were quick to point out that the rise in payrolls could easily outstrip the consensus forecast.
MFR Inc U.S. economist Suzanne Rizzo argued the case for a larger payrolls gain partly by citing the low level of jobless claims and several signs of stronger manufacturing employment.
Rizzo also noted a pick-up in the Conference Board's gauge of consumer confidence in the job market and improvement in the help-wanted index.
The Conference Board reported that 33 percent of households surveyed in March said jobs are "plentiful", up from 32.5 percent in February.
The National Association of Purchasing Management said its employment index rose to 51.6 in March from 45.4 in February.
"I don't see anything at all that tells me employment growth is slowing down at all in March, and I think, the consensus number is saying that it is," Rizzo said.

MFR expects that non-farm payrolls grew by 275,000 in March. "If our forecast comes true, it's probably too strong to be consistent with an economy that is growing slowly enough to avoid accelerating pressures on inflation and wages and prices," Rizzo said.
A hefty 109,000 gain in construction jobs helped swell February payrolls, but analysts do not expect a repeat of the strong gains in construction employment.
Construction employment ought to show another rise, although not as stong as the increase in February, said Dan Seto, a senior economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
Seto put the gain in construction jobs at about 40,000 in March and the rise in overall payrolls at 280,000.
The March employment report comes on the heels of the first Fed interest rate hike in more than two years.
On March 25, Fed policymakers increased the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent.

A statement issued by the Fed said it tightened credit because persistent strength in demand is progressively increasing the risk of inflationary imbalances developing in the economy that would eventually undermine the expansion.
The wording of the Fed statement prompted some analysts to suggest financial markets will focus heavily on payrolls.

"The thing here to keep in mind is that this time around the markets will be looking at non-farm payrolls a lot more than they look at the average hourly earnings, and the reason for that is obvious," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors.
When the Fed tightened rates, the central bank suggested very cleary that it was looking at demand pressures and economic growth, Chan said.
"They didn't talk so much about prices," he added.
Chan also expects that payrolls grew by 280,000 in March.
Analysts also emphasized the importance of the aggregate weekly hours index, a barometer of output which climbed to 140.8 in February from 137.1 in January.

"If that index even just stays at the same level as last month, that points to a 4.0 percent gain on a quarter-to-quarter basis annualized," said Seto adding that generally has implications for gross domestic product (GDP).
"I think if we get a strong report as we project, then you're going to have more people looking at GDP growth in the 3.5 to 4.0 percent range," he added.
In the final quarter of 1996, the economy expanded at a 3.8 percent annualized pace.
